article.title: Black Panthers at 60
article.author: Melina Abdullah
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Over the last several weeks, we have been slapped with the reality that this nation’s systems were never designed to benefit or bring justice to Black people. In fact, the nation was built on our backs and profits from our exploitation and oppression. Most recent verdicts and rulings in the murders of Baby #KohenWiley, #NolanWells, #MarchelloWoodard, Sr. Airman #RogerFortson, #JaylenLewis, and #FrankTyson, are emblematic of the ways in which we are constantly betrayed by the entire (in)justice system. Politicians unleash pol(ICE) to kill at will. Even the best and brightest among us (Karmelo Anthony) are sentenced to lifetimes in cages after being forced to defend themselves from racist violence. All our money is being sent to carry out a genocide in Palestine as people live unhoused on Skid Row. As gas prices, groceries, rents, and electric bills soar, worker salaries are at below-survival levels. White boys at Ivy Leagues are all but greenlit to rape women…and, why not? There is a rapist and pedophile in the White House. Related: Remembering Curtis Renee: Seven Lessons in Love, Liberation, and Revolution As political ads flood the airwaves telling us that the answer lies in flipping Congress (as if most Democrats aren’t also pro-cop, genociders, owned by corporations), we must also remember that Black people have never simply voted ourselves into freedom. We must vote and organize in the Black radical tradition. Last weekend, we celebrated the 60th anniversary of the Black Panther Party, which was birthed in Oakland, California on October 15, 1966 by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale, who were community college students at the time. The Black Panthers are the standard-bearers for what it means to be revolutionaries. They visioned and modeled Black self-defense, liberatory praxis, community building, healing justice, and mutual aid. They built survival programs like freedom schools, community health clinics, and free food programs, many of which were adapted and implemented by local, state, and federal governments. Point five of their ten-point platform serves as the basis for Black Studies, which they organized, fought for, and won alongside students at San Francisco State in 1968. Related: The Case Is Closed. The Fight for Justice for Nolan Wells Is Not. As they exposed and made demands of the system, they raised the collective consciousness, inspired, and directed the revolutionary will of the people. They defined and demonstrated solidarity among oppressed people from Indigenous, Brown, Asian, and even poor white communities in the United States, to people fighting for liberation in Palestine, Cuba, Latin America, Asia, throughout the African continent and diaspora, and around the world. Black Lives Matter Grassroots has been tremendously fortunate to be guided in the Black radical tradition by Black Panther Panther veterans: from the wisdom our founding Board member “Baba” Hank Jones, to BLM Detroit co-founder Curtis Renee’s father Wayne Curtis, to the family ties with Geronimo Jijaga Pratt and our Gary chapter, to the constant presence and teachings of Dr. Mutulu Shakur, Baba Sekou Odinga and Dedon Kamathi until their passing, the wisdoms of Ericka Huggins, Yasmeen Majid, Emory Douglas, and Jihad Abdulmumit, to the healing justice work of Mama Trudy Goodwin inside BLMLA, the mentoring of Martin Gordon in Pasadena, Black August commemorations with Comrade Harold Welton and the LA Panthers, and the ongoing work alongside Black Panther Party Cub Chairman Fred Hampton, Jr. At a time when the world is heading to hell in a handbasket, celebrating 60 years of the Black Panther Party must not only take the form of panels, dinners, street-namings, and concerts – which were, by all means, significant and important. We must also be inspired by a legacy that returns us to a radical Black power praxis. Related: Old Is Not Ugly: Jasmine Guy and the Politics of Aging While Black As we vote on Election Day, we must identify and uphold our own moral minimums and only vote for candidates and measures that are in line. (For me, that’s: F the Pol(ICE), Reparations Now, Free Palestine, People Over Profits, Liberated Ethnic Studies, Free the Land, and Solidarity Forever.) We learn from the Black Panther Party that, even the most aligned politicians and policies can only serve as stop-gaps. Electoral politics and policy work at its best offers non-reformist reform. It takes more than that to free us. So, we celebrate the Black Panther Party and inherit their legacy by grounding ourselves in the understanding that society must be transformed. Only the people can do that. We are the people who must vision, organize, and undertake that work. All power to the people! Los Angeles Sentinel
